cim: Why Higher Ed Technology Leaders Should Pay Attention to Question Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Why Higher Ed Technology Leaders Should Pay Attention to Question Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Consider this scenario: A student raises a hand in class and asks a question about an assignment. The instructor guides the student to an answer. The exchange appears complete. Yet a closer look at the student’s question may reveal something more useful to the instructor: The assignment directions may not be as clear as intended.

Across higher education, these exchanges happen every day. Their immediate value is easy to recognize. Students receive answers that help them understand course content, navigate requirements and make decisions. However, the value of the questions students ask to faculty and staff deserves equal attention. These questions can reveal where assignment explanations fall short, policies are misunderstood or additional learning support may be needed — and the questions students don’t ask can signal a need for faculty intervention.

I call the approach to turning these signals into actionable insights “Question Intelligence,” or QI. For higher education technology leaders, QI offers a new opportunity to learn from the questions people ask, and don’t ask, about their institutional courses, programs, webpages, policies and services.

I define QI as the systematic interpretation of patterns in the questions people ask, and don’t ask, relative to human-defined expectations. From my perspective, a QI system, artificial intelligence-based or otherwise, should always aim to recognize meaningful and emergent question patterns and turn them into actionable insights for early decision-making and timely responses.

The human-defined expectations matter. Faculty expect students to develop a clear understanding of the content they teach. University administrators expect students, staff and faculty to understand the content they place across campus webpages, institutional policies and academic calendars. QI can help faculty and administrators check those assertions by surfacing patterns in the questions people ask about content.

A QI system serves a different purpose than a chatbot. A chatbot may successfully answer the same question dozens of times while the underlying source of confusion remains unchanged. QI brings the sources of confusion to the attention of a designated faculty or staff member, creating an earlier opportunity for them to respond with a targeted intervention.

Faculty are not mind readers. They cannot respond to questions students never ask. While faculty may eventually recognize hidden or unexpressed student confusion through lagging indicators, such as graded assignments and examinations, these insights often come too late. By the time confusion becomes visible, it may have already negatively affected student learning and academic performance.

Consider an assignment that requires something students suddenly realize they do not yet understand. At 11 p.m., with their instructor unavailable, the students turn to a course chatbot for help. The chatbot uses Socratic questioning to guide them toward understanding while leaving the work in their hands.

The next morning, an integrated QI system draws the instructor’s attention to a pattern in the questions students asked the chatbot. The pattern signals the source of the shared misunderstanding. Alerted by the QI system, the instructor comes prepared to address the source in the very next class, before the assignment deadline.

The benefit here is early notice of student confusion. One small instructional adjustment or response, delivered at the right time, could prevent student confusion from compounding over an entire semester.

The same QI benefit extends to administrative offices. Publishing a faculty handbook, university policy, event calendar, or tenure and promotion guidelines does not guarantee that readers will understand the content within.

For example, the registrar’s office might list the process for course registration on its webpage, yet students and academic advisers may repeatedly ask for clarification. An integrated QI system could capture those questions, analyze and signal the sources of confusion, and prompt designated staff to add suggested information to the webpage or host a targeted information session.

Senior leaders in higher education could also use QI systems to gain greater visibility into what the public asks, and does not ask, about their institution. This new data could help strengthen recruitment efforts, identify communication gaps, guide improvements to campus webpages and coordinate timely outreach. Addressing underlying confusion could also reduce recurring questions in their inboxes.

DISCOVER: Higher ed IT teams can help reduce friction in digital experiences.

QI system evaluations should go beyond determining effective and meaningful pattern recognition. Did the QI system surface human-validated sources of confusion? Were QI insights meaningful to designated faculty and staff? Did human response improve collective understanding? Participating institutions should also assess QI system data privacy, user interface accessibility and ease of interpretation.

One early example of QI in practice is LectureLoop, an AI-powered educational tool I developed that provides students with a private, 24/7 channel to ask questions about faculty-approved course content while helping faculty identify patterns in what students ask, and don’t ask, about that content.

In a pilot program, the results of which were presented at EDUCAUSE 2026, students used the platform to seek clarification and learning support beyond traditional classroom interactions. Survey findings suggested promising improvements across several self-reported dimensions of learning. More important, the pilot demonstrated a broader possibility: Educational chatbots can do more than answer students’ questions. They can also help educators learn from patterns in those questions, identify emerging areas of confusion and intervene before misunderstandings become persistent barriers to learning.

Through LectureLoop, I am seeking faculty and institutional partners interested in exploring these questions via structured beta testing. Findings from this work could help clarify where QI adds value and what responsible, practical QI systems should look like.
